In this work, we introduce 𝒍𝒊𝒗𝒆 𝒏𝒐𝒊𝒔𝒆 𝒇𝒊𝒏𝒈𝒆𝒓𝒑𝒓𝒊𝒏𝒕𝒊𝒏𝒈, a lightweight and empirical approach to characterising noisy quantum systems.

Software testability has been a foundational concept in software engineering for decades, shaping how we reason about fault detection, debugging, and software quality. Yet, despite rapid advances in quantum computing, there has been no formal notion of testability for quantum software.

In this work, we take a first step toward closing that gap by introducing the 𝐟𝐢𝐫𝐬𝐭 𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐦𝐚𝐥𝐢𝐬𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐨𝐟 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐧𝐭𝐮𝐦 𝐬𝐨𝐟𝐭𝐰𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐭𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐲. Building on classical software engineering and quantum information theory, we define 𝑸𝒖𝒂𝒏𝒕𝒖𝒎 𝑺𝒒𝒖𝒆𝒆𝒛𝒊𝒏𝒆𝒔𝒔—an information-theoretic measure that captures how much information about a fault is lost as it propagates through a quantum program.

The key idea is simple: if faults are masked before they reach observable outcomes, the software becomes harder to test. Quantum Squeeziness quantifies this phenomenon, providing a rigorous foundation for reasoning about fault propagation, observability, and test effectiveness in quantum systems. Across 50,000+ mutants, we show that higher squeeziness strongly predicts lower fault detectability, while our optimized 𝑭𝒂𝒔𝒕𝑺𝒒𝒖𝒆𝒆𝒛𝒊𝒏𝒆𝒔𝒔 technique achieves a 16.9× speedup with 95% accuracy.

#QuantumComputing | #QEC | #FaultTolerance | #RealTimeSystems | #QuantumMachines | #NonClifford | #IEEE To view or add a comment, sign in Some time ago, I read a quantum error correction paper that really caught my attention. It focused on a specific adaptive syndrome measurement protocol, but the broader takeaway was what got me excited: classical feedforward can be used to drastically reduce logical errors.

It also forced me to rethink a lot of what I knew about decoding. Specifically, decoding hypergraphs (which are used alongside the syndrome to accurately correct errors) could no longer be built ahead of time. They had to be assembled just-in-time. Otherwise, memory requirements scale exponentially, making static setups completely impractical for most real-world systems.

Of course, many of us rely on Stim to generate detector error models and compile decoding hypergraphs. But its execution latency is simply too high for online, just-in-time generation, even on “slow-clock” platforms like neutral atom and trapped ion systems.

In our recent paper, we propose a parallel formulation of Stim’s backtracking algorithm and implement it in a new GPU-accelerated compiler called GreenPeas. On select benchmarks, it achieves a geometric mean speedup of 13.2× over Stim, enabling adaptive circuit simulations and deployments that were previously impractical.

Example: we circuit-level decoded [[4, 2, 2]]-concatenated surface codes with adaptive syndrome measurements by building decoding hypergraphs on-the-fly with GreenPeas. The result: 6.7× fewer logical errors and 4.5× faster decoding relative to prior phenomenological approaches.

GreenPeas is fully open-source. If you know C (and some of the good parts of C++), please consider contributing.

Combining work and study is manageable. But in practice, there are a few challenges that need to be addressed.

For me, most of the friction came from three places:

𝟭. 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝘅𝘁 𝘀𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴

Switching ways of thinking is expensive.

At work, the mindset is broad, fast, and adaptive: people, business, technology, decisions. In academia, it is about depth: concept after concept, detail after detail.

Both matter. But moving between them has a cost.

My tip: acknowledge that context switching costs time and energy, reduce it where you can, and take it into account when planning so you do not overload yourself.

𝟮. 𝗢𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗶𝘁𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴

Saying yes feels like progress, especially when you are involved in more than one world.

There are interesting opportunities everywhere, but the main pillars still need most of the attention.

For me, overcommitting usually leads to more context switching and general overload.

My tip: choose one or two main pillars, such as work and study, and give them most of your focus. Other commitments can stay, but in a lighter form and with clearer boundaries.

𝟯. 𝗣𝗿𝗶𝗼𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗶𝘇𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻

It is not enough to prioritize between work and study. You also need to prioritize within each one.

The main task, the important project at work, the fundamental course at university: these heavy-weight tasks usually carry most of the value.

My tip: focus on where the impact is highest, not only on what feels urgent.

I am still learning how to make this more sustainable.

Excited to share our new paper on arXiv: Anticipating Decoder Side-channel Attacks in Fault-tolerant Quantum Computers By Shashvat S., Dan E. Browne, Shin Nishio https://lnkd.in/e8dcujKd

As quantum computing emerges as an applied technology, there is a growing need to protect quantum computers against information security attacks. This work identifies a new class of side-channel attacks against fault-tolerant quantum computers, in which the syndrome data that is sent to the decoder system is used to infer which computation (logical circuit) is taking place on the quantum computer. Our work introduces the concept of gate fingerprints, which describes those patterns present in syndrome data that indicate which logical operation took place on the quantum computer. We show different effects by which logical operations produce gate fingerprints by focusing on Clifford+T computation in the surface code. We then explore how gate fingerprint information can be used to make inferences about the circuits or algorithms run on a quantum computer. Our findings indicate that decoder systems can be a vector for side-channel attacks, and thus, to prevent this, decoder systems should either be secured or built by a trusted party.

Many thanks to my co-authors for the great collaboration!

Software testability has been a foundational concept in software engineering for decades, shaping how we reason about fault detection, debugging, and software quality. Yet, despite rapid advances in quantum computing, there has been no formal notion of testability for quantum software.

To view or add a comment, sign in Some time ago, I read a quantum error correction paper that really caught my attention. It focused on a specific adaptive syndrome measurement protocol, but the broader takeaway was what got me excited: classical feedforward can be used to drastically reduce logical errors.

It also forced me to rethink a lot of what I knew about decoding. Specifically, decoding hypergraphs (which are used alongside the syndrome to accurately correct errors) could no longer be built ahead of time. They had to be assembled just-in-time. Otherwise, memory requirements scale exponentially, making static setups completely impractical for most real-world systems.

Of course, many of us rely on Stim to generate detector error models and compile decoding hypergraphs. But its execution latency is simply too high for online, just-in-time generation, even on “slow-clock” platforms like neutral atom and trapped ion systems.

In our recent paper, we propose a parallel formulation of Stim’s backtracking algorithm and implement it in a new GPU-accelerated compiler called GreenPeas. On select benchmarks, it achieves a geometric mean speedup of 13.2× over Stim, enabling adaptive circuit simulations and deployments that were previously impractical.

In general, a qubit can only encode one bit of information (due to Holevo’s Theorem). So, if Alice wants to send 2 classical bits of information to Bob using qubits, she must send 2 of them. But let’s consider superdense coding for a moment. Superdense coding is a protocol in quantum information that allows Alice to send 2 classical bits by sending one qubit, provided that they both already share an EPR pair (i.e. a maximally entangled pair of qubits). I’ll link a more complete explanation of superdense coding in the comments.

So, one way to think about superdense coding is the following:

  1. Alice prepares an EPR pair.
  2. Alice sends half the EPR pair (1 qubit) to Bob.
  3. Alice encodes the 2 bits in her qubit by applying some operation on it.
  4. Alice sends the qubit to Bob.
  5. Bob decodes the “new” qubit along with the “old” one and extracts 2 bits.

This seems pretty straightforward, and makes intuitive sense: Alice effectively sends 2 qubits to Bob, so in terms of capacity, it is no wonder she can “exchange” these 2 qubits with two bits.

But what happens if we look at the same protocol a bit differently? What if instead of Alice preparing the initial EPR pair, Bob produces it, and then sends one qubit to Alice. The protocol is still exactly the same, since our pre-condition is that Alice and Bob share an EPR pair. However, this time, Alice only ever sends one qubit to Bob, but still manages to transmit 2 bits of information!

Of course, this doesn’t violate Holevo’s Theorem - since Alice and Bob do share an EPR pair to begin with, which assists in increasing the classical capacity.

This perspective was first brought to my attention by my supervisor, Michael Ben-Or, and it is one of those cool examples where entanglement kind of “breaks” the classical intuition. In the last post, we talked about waves and interference. We said that the goal of a quantum algorithm is to make useful answers “stronger” and useless answers fade, before measurement. But what does “stronger” actually mean?

In quantum computing, we do not directly see all the possible answers. When we measure, we only get one result. So “stronger” does not mean the answer is visible during the computation. It means that a useful answer becomes more likely to appear when we measure.

This is where interference becomes important. During the computation, the quantum state evolves. Different possible evolutions of the quantum state can interfere with each other. Some possible states reinforce certain outcomes, making them more likely to appear when we measure.

A good quantum algorithm that exploits interference is designed so that, by the end: • useful answers have higher probability • less useful answers have lower probability Then we measure. And if the algorithm works as intended, the result is more likely to be the correct answer.

This is very different from a classical algorithm. A classical algorithm usually tries to identify the answer step by step. A quantum algorithm shapes the probabilities before the final measurement.

So again, quantum algorithms are not about “trying all answers at once”. They are about carefully guiding interference to make useful answers more likely.

Software testability has been a foundational concept in software engineering for decades, shaping how we reason about fault detection, debugging, and software quality. Yet, despite rapid advances in quantum computing, there has been no formal notion of testability for quantum software. In this work, we take a first step toward closing that gap by introducing the 𝐟𝐢𝐫𝐬𝐭 𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐦𝐚𝐥𝐢𝐬𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐨𝐟 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐧𝐭𝐮𝐦 𝐬𝐨𝐟𝐭𝐰𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐭𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐲. 🎉 Excited to share that my first journal paper has been accepted at ACM TOSEM!

🌱 This paper is more than a publication—it reflects how much I’ve learned about research and communication along the way.

Good research is more than results When I started this project—the first of my PhD—I thought success meant getting the methods right and producing solid results. That alone took about a year. What I didn’t anticipate was that learning how to explain why those results mattered would take just as long. I presented this work in very different contexts: in Oxford to quantum physicists and chemists, in Copenhagen to non-quantum software researchers, and in Montpellier to quantum algorithms experts. In each community, a few people with very different backgrounds paused to bridge their perspective with this work. That led to rich discussions. The most fascinating part was aligning our vocabularies and finding shared ground. After each conference, I reshaped the paper with these new perspectives in mind. 💭 At one conference, I met a professor I deeply admire. We jumped straight into a technical discussion. She assumed I had a similar background—and I didn’t pause to explain that while our areas are related, we approach problems differently. She eventually walked away saying my work felt neither theoretical nor practical. That moment stuck with me. It was frustrating, unsettling, and honestly quite disorienting, but it now guides how I explain results.

Quantum software research is about communication The same challenge appeared during the review process. No reviewer questioned the methodology or results. Instead, feedback focused on framing, context, and narrative. Comparing the first version with the current one—shaped by reviews and discussions—the difference is massive. 🔗 I realized this isn’t a secondary skill. In interdisciplinary fields like quantum computing, communication is part of the research itself. This is especially true for quantum software research: still underexplored, yet crucial for moving from lab-scale demonstrations to industrial pipelines and real-world use cases. Building that bridge isn’t just about better hardware or algorithms—it’s about elegant software that smartly connects the two, layers of abstraction, fault understanding, and, above all, a shared language across communities.

Interdisciplinary collaboration drives innovation Working across quantum physics, chemistry, and software engineering taught me that breakthroughs often happen at the intersections. When experts from different fields try to connect perspectives, new questions arise, assumptions are challenged, and insights emerge that wouldn’t have been possible within a single discipline. Each discussion shaped the paper and, more importantly, shaped how I think as a researcher.

🙏 Grateful to my supervisors and co-authors for their support. Excited—and a bit wiser—to enter my final PhD year. There’s a lot coming!

🙏 I'm honored to share that two of our papers have been accepted at OOPSLA 2025! It's been a long and exciting journey, and I'm thrilled to see our work recognized at this top venue.

🔬 The first paper, AccelerQ: Accelerating Quantum Eigensolvers With Machine Learning on Quantum Simulators, reframes the challenge of tuning NISQ (Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum) algorithms as a hyperparameter optimization problem — opening the door for the software engineering and ML communities to engage with quantum algorithm optimisation in novel ways.

🧪 The second, Shaking Up Quantum Simulators with Fuzzing and Rigour, introduces a powerful combination of fuzz testing and formal methods to systematically uncover bugs in quantum simulators — pushing for more reliable quantum software stacks.

🌏 Looking forward to presenting both papers in Singapore and connecting with the amazing SPLASH/OOPSLA community. See you there!
